author: reek
body: UefiConsole wraps the firmware's text-in and text-out protocols. Most of it is decision rather than device: a key arrives with a code and a modifier mask, and the chapter's job is to say which of forty-odd predicates that key satisfies. Attributes and pixels are the same shape of work -- packing named colours into the bit layout the firmware expects.

author: reek
body: THIS TEST WAS WRITTEN AGAINST A CONTRACT THAT NO LONGER EXISTS, and it did not fail quietly: main 10550 deleted the `uefi-scan-*` table and every one of those names became CDX3002. So the test stopped compiling rather than stopping being true, which is the good failure of the two. Red found it with the first instrumented `-All`.

author: reek
body: What is NOT covered here, deliberately: uefi-console-init reads the SystemTable through peek-qword, and uefi-con-move and friends call into ConOut. Those need firmware, and a test that pretended otherwise would be reading whatever address zero happens to hold. This pins the half that is arithmetic, and says so rather than implying the chapter is covered.

author: reek
body: The builder mirrors `uefi-key-of`, which is the one place a UefiKey is built in the shipping path: scan-code and char-code are both the raw poll-key value, and shift-state is poll-mods with the validity bit set. A fixture that filled those fields any other way would be testing a shape the producer never emits.

author: reek
body: The unvalidated builder exists for exactly one reading. The firmware sets the validity bit to say the modifier field means anything at all, and `uefi-key-is-ctrl-alt-del` gates on it, so a reboot combo that fires on an unset modifier field is the failure worth pinning.

author: reek
body: Each key is described by the NAMES of every predicate it satisfies, not by a count. A count would pass if two predicates swapped which key they answered to; the names would not. It also means a named key that answered `char` as well as itself is visible in the line rather than hidden behind a total.

author: reek
body: Every named key is asked with no modifiers, so its line must carry its own name and NOTHING else. That is the reading that separates a working predicate set from one where two predicates compare against the same constant: a duplicated comparison shows up as two names on one line.

author: reek
body: `insert` is asked even though `uefi-key-is-insert` is hardcoded False, because KeyInput has no named key for it. The line proves the honest False rather than leaving a predicate nobody exercises; if Insert is ever given a named key, this line is where the wiring gets noticed.

author: reek
body: A Ctrl chord is the letter plus the ctrl bit, and `key-upper` folds the case so it fires whether or not shift is held. Both cases are asked, and the last two lines are the ones that make the chord a chord: the same letter without the ctrl bit must NOT fire, and ctrl with a different letter must not fire either.

author: reek
body: The two ctrl-alt-delete lines differ in one bit: the second omits the validity flag. Ctrl+Alt+Del in the dev console never fired for years because every constructor left shift-state at zero, so the predicate was False unconditionally; the validated line is what proves it fires at all and the unvalidated line is what proves the gate still holds.
